scope: Deeper reverse engineering of the opaque cases from the initial 100-file review. This is not a claim that all 20 initial holds are closed.
method: Static PE/.NET/Go analysis, archive and string decoding, plus bounded Unicorn CPU models with explicitly recorded synthetic API returns and conditional assumptions. No sample was launched natively; no sample endpoint was contacted.

tools.optional_unavailable: Ghidra files exist, but no Java runtime was available. This did not block the recovered evidence.

findings: 7z extraction exposed enCrAshReP.dll, SHA256 07998a616b57975e656fef18092559ac04f87b1ebf1493958fa64a3f2c08f66f. Export metadata names MSEdgeWebView.dll; most crash-reporting exports alias one obfuscated entry.
At VA 0x1000fe08, UTF-16 key and hexadecimal strings are converted to narrow strings; 0x1000fd24 hex-decodes and RC4-decrypts them. The key comes from data passed by the callers, not brute force.

Recovered strings include the CMSTPLUA elevation moniker, ComputerDefaults.exe, the ms-settings shell-open command key, and DelegateExecute. The moniker flows to CoGetObject at 0x1000d777 and interface slot 0x24 at 0x1000d7a3.
Recovered driver paths include \.\MonProcessEX, \.\DCRCVDRV_U, and \.\ardrv. Separate decrypted lists name antivirus and EDR processes, including Defender, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, and K7 products.

The list at raw 0x197908 is split into process names. VA 0x1000b20a enumerates processes and returns a matching PID. VA 0x1000868a pushes each selected PID, 0x1000868c pushes IOCTL 0x02420031, and 0x1000aa35 passes the PID as a four-byte input to DeviceIoControl.
A separate helper at 0x1000b8e7 resolves VirtualAllocEx, allocates remote RWX memory, and calls WriteProcessMemory.
Original-image recognition and recursive extraction are now verified: fresh Atomscan identifies VHD, scans the DLL, and rolls up the three suspicious traits. See format-dispatch.json.
remaining_limits: Automatic driver-target/control-flow rules remain incomplete; container extraction is no longer the blocker.

The target-driver implementation and protected export dispatcher were not fully recovered. The driver-kill interpretation is supported by target selection and IOCTL flow, not an observed runtime termination.

samples.assessment: hidden HTTP command agent; recommended bad
findings: Go build information names mcp-agent; analyzed function symbols belong to main, rather than merely being embedded strings.
The main task loop calls getTasks at 0x68d740, executeTask at 0x68d7ad, and sendResult at 0x68d857. getTasks issues an HTTP GET; sendResult JSON-encodes and POSTs the returned task result.
The controller is https://138.124.123.56:8443 with /checkin, /tasks/, and /results routes. No endpoint was contacted.

The shell task passes its command to shellExec. At 0x68c2a3 the code calls os/exec.Command with cmd /c and the supplied command. It sets HideWindow and CREATE_NO_WINDOW, invokes CombinedOutput in a goroutine, and kills the child on timeout.

Other dispatched tasks include directory listing, reading/downloading files, writing uploaded files, host information, sleep, and exit. The reviewed paths use Client.Get/Post without an application-level task approval check.
remaining_limits: No operator authorization or deployment provenance is present in these bytes. The review proves the hidden command/result channel; it does not prove who deployed it.
Current automatic findings do not express the complete remote task-to-shell-to-result data flow.

samples.assessment: benign Eldara game trainer; good with one unusual finding
findings: Managed IL identifies EldaraTrainer.Program and methods for Steam discovery, debug endpoint polling, target selection, WebSocket evaluation, and bundle expansion.
Launch arguments select Steam app 4746070 and bind the DevTools endpoint to 127.0.0.1:9229. The code waits for the game target and sends Runtime.evaluate through its local WebSocket.
The UTF-16 Base64/GZIP string at raw offset 12372 expands to 241045 bytes of JavaScript, SHA256 f1d4195ec595a8fd866c1832de249baf0b811cf1dd285e4af97230809d847667.

The decoded modules implement game controls for items, world, utility, forge, combat, progression, hunting, appearance and UI. Storage operations concern game saves/settings. Managed code and the decoded bundle showed no external controller or credential-collection path.

Fresh Atomscan reports one distinct suspicious ID, binary/embedded/base64-gz, repeated at parent and extracted-child levels; no hostile ID. The initial review incorrectly counted these two occurrences as two distinct findings.
remaining_limits: This is a static review of the supplied build, not a runtime guarantee or a statement about game rules.

samples.assessment: Cobalt Strike Beacon implant; routed bad (Hopper noop)
findings: The raw bootstrap is executable MZRE-prefixed x86 code. Its call/pop/add sequence invokes the reflective loader at raw 0x9436.

e_lfanew points to raw 0x100, where the normal PE signature was replaced by TL followed by two zero bytes. Changing only those four bytes in an analysis copy reveals a coherent PE32 DLL exporting _ReflectiveLoader@4; the original was not modified.

XOR 0x2e at raw 0x33a20 yields a 4096-byte configuration with more than 50 well-formed big-endian TLV fields, an RSA public key, the ns1.blueorbits.site controller string, process paths and DNS prefixes.
The normalized copy matches three hostile detections, including Beacon-loader and Cobalt Strike YARA signatures. The decoded configuration independently corroborates that identification.

Bounded structural validation in Cleave now preserves PE dispatch despite the damaged signature. Fresh Atomscan on the unchanged original emits two hostile Cobalt Strike signatures and three suspicious findings. See damaged-pe-dispatch.json; all 20 dispatch tests and the current full validation suite pass.
remaining_limits: Filefacts still reports a PE parse failure, so native semantic facts remain incomplete. Raw-byte and tampering detectors now run correctly.

samples.assessment: keep purgatory; unsupported family conclusions removed
findings: The 6833257-byte artifact contains dozens of appended PE headers. Version/export inspection identifies Java policytool/servertool, UPX, Adobe helpers, Firefox plugin-hang-ui, MavInject, SetupHost, DiagTrackRunner, Windows setup and boot components, alongside unresolved members.

The first 0x179ff bytes repeat identically at raw 0x2e8b75. Multiple member boundaries occur one byte before the preceding declared raw-image end. This is a repeated collection layout, not by itself an execution chain.
No reviewed outer-to-appended-payload control-flow link establishes HijackLoader. Two family composites used only names/layout and loose member API co-occurrence; both have been removed.

Post-change Atomscan retains exactly the two suspicious structural findings: non-executable-writable-entry-pe-carrier and high-entropy-reloc-overhang. No blanket benign exception or underlying capability suppression was added.
remaining_limits: Several appended members have malformed imports or unresolved code. The collection is not cleared for the good pool.
No malicious family or execution outcome is asserted solely from filenames or PE co-occurrence.

findings: 7z identifies an appended SquashFS 4.0 filesystem at raw offset 188392, containing an Electron application and resources/app.asar.
ASAR header parsing extracted 13305 stored files. Cleave analyzed 16009 records including derived children, with zero suspicious or hostile IDs; AppRun also has no high findings.
Package metadata identifies Repath Studio 0.4.26, a vector graphics editor. Included source maps recover the Electron main/preload/file modules.

Reviewed main-process IPC provides document open/save/print and window controls. External links require HTTPS and an explicit host allowlist. The main process initializes Sentry and electron-updater, and loads a local renderer.
All 13 extracted ELF binaries have completed Atomscan reports with no high findings. The complete ASAR and launcher passed a separate current-Cleave scan; see appimage-coverage.json.
remaining_limits: The outer AppImage format still is not automatically traversed by the normal scanner. This decision uses explicit extraction and complete executable-component coverage.
The redundant full-tree Atomscan was stopped after all native members completed; its unfinished repeat of the ASAR is not represented as a completed scan.

samples.assessment: encrypted in-memory callback loader; recommended bad
findings: NSIS extraction yields Signs plus large sparse companion files. Refinery xtnsis also recovers setup.nsis, which ordinary 7z extraction omits.

The installer constructs Kernel32 API names by taking every third character starting at index 2. Decoded calls open Signs, allocate memory with allocation type 0x3000 and protection 0x40, then ReadFile into that buffer.
It adds 11024 to the buffer pointer and passes that address as the EnumResourceTypesA callback. This binds opaque file bytes to executable control flow.

The callback decoder copies 0x1f01c bytes from Signs offset 0x4403 and XORs dwords with 0x786c749a. The resulting 127004-byte stage has SHA256 d87c43e225824a6aae3bb4613a448c66669e6b363d91b4fe144464fb67effc3b.

Bounded CPU-only emulation of that decoded arithmetic executes 189186 instructions before the first PEB read at stage offset 0x1b16d. No OS model, imports, filesystem, network, or native process execution was supplied.
Static inspection shows PEB/module traversal and an XOR-word routine searching for an MZ result. This establishes another loader stage, not a recovered final malware family.

Follow-up hash-checked tracing reaches registration of the handler at stage+0x1e37b. Direct CPU checks verify five exception codes and the transformation EIP += byte(EIP+20) XOR 0x19. A nonzero Dr0 causes a secondary invalid read in the handler model; it does not cleanly return SEARCH.

The API hash routine at 0x1d9bf was directly checked for five names, including RtlAddVectoredExceptionHandler, NtAllocateVirtualMemory, and ZwQueryVirtualMemory. Under the recorded synthetic returns, the trace reaches two allocation calls and a process-memory query.
The memory scanner at 0x1d33b walks 4 KiB pages and compares six printable-string length/hash pairs. The marker texts are unresolved.

A separate trace explicitly assuming no memory-marker match reaches a far jump through selector 0x33 to 64-bit code at stage+0x1c9a2. Static inspection of that block shows a native PEB debug-byte check with an infinite loop on the nonzero branch. See nsis-control-flow.json and the portable trace model.

The portable mixed-mode model validates the selector-0x33 entry and selector-0x23 return. In a synthetic Windows 10 environment the x64 block executes 28,901 instructions, requests native memory protection (syscall 0x50), scans a NOP-filled native DLL text section, and returns to x86. The x86 continuation resolves ExitProcess and NtProtectVirtualMemory and reaches another protection call. See nsis-control-flow.json for every assumption and the stop boundary.
remaining_limits: Mixed-mode tracing stops at stage+0x1c02c when synthetic DLL code lacks a searched patch target, producing address 0xfffffffb. Real target-code semantics are still required; no final payload recovery is claimed.
The relationship to the sparse companion files remains unresolved.
The production NSIS path still omits its installer instruction stream, leaving the callback-loading chain undetected.

findings: All four images have the same common prefix except a 16-byte mutation slot at 0x126cc..0x126db after [[UNIQUE]]. Their differing lengths are truncations/extensions of the same underlying image, not four independent behaviors.
A bounded UPX-decoder emulation stopped at 0x42871c before import resolution or application execution. It recovers the outer self-submission code, consistent with the prior exact-overlay review.

The outer program reads its own file, mutates the 16-byte slot, uploads the clone as a multipart file, deletes it and repeats. This does not prove victim-file exfiltration or execution of the appended PE.
An embedded PE starts at 0x14c8b. The index-62 overlay SHA256 5350dc736d0b67b0d39ea24d57194d795d9f3614d7f994b252ccfa9587ed8991 exactly matches testdata/triage/02d544dd-self-submission/review.json.

The appended native CLR-hosting code references mscoree/CLRCreateInstance and encrypted resources. RCDATA __ declares 1937627 bytes but only a prefix is present; the separate 32-byte ~ resource is absent in every copy. The shortest copy does not contain the resource directory at all.
The exact available resource lengths are reproduced in recovered.json. Missing bytes, rather than missing reverse-engineering tools, prevent a complete embedded-managed-payload verdict.
remaining_limits: No available copy contains the missing key/resource tail. No benign or hostile conclusion is invented for absent payload bytes.
